title: The Christmas truce (1914)
hook: soldiers climb out of the trenches to sing carols and share food with the enemy
carry: silent night in no man's land

segments.voice: Yesterday, the new martyrs of Russia, witnesses in the camps. Your line was faithful in the camps. What small hidden faithful thing did you do? Day nine hundred forty-five.

A cold, clear Christmas Eve in Flanders. Two lines of trenches, close enough to shout across. Between them, a strip of mud, wire and shell holes the soldiers call no man's land. Anyone who raises his head above the parapet risks a bullet. Then, on the German side, lights appear: small candles, and in places little Christmas trees set up along the trench. A voice starts singing, and others join. Stille Nacht. Silent night. On the British side, men listen. After a while, someone sings back. Today, what happened next.

Much of what we know comes from soldiers' letters home. In places along the line, men climbed out of their trenches, unarmed, and walked toward each other. They shook hands. They swapped what they had: chocolate, cigarettes, sausage, buttons from their uniforms, addresses to write to after the war. Some letters mention a kick-about with a ball. Both sides used the quiet to bury their dead, and in places they held services together over the graves. Then the truce ended, and the shooting started again. Honesty matters here. It didn't happen everywhere. In some sections, the shooting never stopped. Officers on both sides disapproved, and it was not repeated the same way. So why does it matter? Because of what the soldiers sang. The carols told a story both sides knew: the angels over the shepherds' fields, singing, in the King James Bible, "Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace, good will toward men." Men who had been trying to kill each other found that they shared a song, a prayer and a holiday. Jesus once said, "Love your enemies." For a night, in a muddy field, some men did. This week, people kept stepping across something. Azusa Street, where the color line washed away. Pandita Ramabai, a home for widows. Sundar Singh, water in an Indian cup. Harris, the walking prophet. Kimbangu, a church from a prison. The martyrs, faithful in the camps. And now enemies sharing chocolate between the trenches.

Here's the practice: share something with an opponent. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind someone you're on the other side of. A rival at work. A relative you argue with. Someone who votes the other way. Notice the trench you've both dug. Now picture a small truce: one thing you could hand across. A compliment you actually mean. A cup of coffee. A question asked out of real curiosity. You don't have to end the war. Just climb out for a moment. If you pray, you can pray for them by name. The bell holds the time.
The Christmas truce. The night soldiers on opposite sides of the trenches sang carols, crossed no man's land, and shared what they had.
Your line: silent night in no man's land. Today, hand one small good thing across to someone you're at odds with, and see what they hand back. Day nine hundred forty-five.

howItsDone: At Christmas, churches sing carols such as Silent Night, and some retell the Christmas truce in services that pray for peace between enemies.
